new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule. Thelwall states only that the Daju languages he recorded (Sila, Nyala, Lagowa, Shatt, Liguri) are not tonal and that the vowel duration he transcribed may reflect stressed syllables; position of stress is not stated. Baygo/Bego was not in his corpus and no source gives any stress information for it.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level remark about five Daju languages other than Bego; the only Baygo materials (MacMichael 1920/1922 and Santandrea 1948 wordlists) say nothing about stress, accent or tone. Not a Baygo statement and not usable for the catalog as one.
new_statements.identity_note: Baygo = Bego/Beigo/Beygo/Bayko (self-name Beoge), a section of Nyala (Darfur) Daju per Stevenson/Thelwall; closest described relative is Dar Fur Daju darf1239 (Nyala, Lagowa). Thelwall's stress remark covers Dar Sila Daju dars1235, Dar Fur Daju darf1239 (Nyala, Lagowa), Shatt shat1244 and Logorik/Liguri logo1261, not bayg1239.

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record for bayg1239. The one statement held by the project (Thelwall 1981: 173, group-level, Bego not in his corpus) says the Daju languages are 'not tonal' and that his double vowels 'may well indicate my perception of stressed syllables' (reading none found). Tucker & Bryan 1966: 232 is compatible on stress (perceived as possibly significant, uninvestigated, no placement) and so adds an earlier, independent group-level remark of the same kind; it differs mildly on tone ('three tone levels have been noted, but no tonal doublets have been found' vs Thelwall's 'not tonal'), a hedged difference recorded under conflicts, not a contradiction about stress placement since neither sourc…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level sketch of the Daju languages (data mainly Stevenson's Shatt; western division 'DAJU' = Darfur/Sila/Lagowa Daju, plus Njalgulgule). The authors note three pitch levels but no tonal minimal pairs, leave examples unmarked for tone, and say stress 'would also seem to have some importance, but has not been fully investigated'. No statement of where stress falls, whether it is contrastive, or how it interacts with the pitch levels. Baygo (Bego/Beigo) is not shown to be named in the chapter: a Google Books full-text probe for 'Bego' with Shatt/Liguri/Sila returned neither Tucker & Bryan volume, while the same route does index the 1956 companion volume for 'Njalgulgule'; the archive.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the section is two sentences long
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's chapter treats the Daju group as a whole ('Eastern: SHATT and LIGURI; Western: DAJU and NJALGULGULE'), with most examples from Stevenson's Shatt material and western examples labelled SILA; Baygo/Bego, an extinct or near-extinct Daju variety south-east of Nyala known only from MacMichael's 1920 wordlist (reprinted by Santandrea 1948), is not shown to be named in the 1966 chapter (the 1956 companion volume and Thelwall 1981 list Bego under Nyala/Darfur Daju). Any stress statement applied to bayg1239 from this work is therefore an inference from the group sketch, not a description of Baygo.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement about stress placement, because no source gives one. The only tension is about tone at Daju-group level: Tucker & Bryan 1966: 232 report that 'three tone levels have been noted, but no tonal doublets have been found', whereas the statement held by the project (Thelwall 1981: 173) says 'these languages are not tonal' and reads vowel doubling as possibly his perception of stress (and Starostin 2016 GLD p. 4, held, says 'Daju languages are not tonal, but stress is distinctive'). Both 1966 and 1981 remarks are hedged, group-level, and based on languages other than Baygo (Shatt mainly for Tucker & Bryan; Sila/Nyala/Lagowa/Shatt/Liguri for Thelwall). Nothing contradicts the catalog, which has no record for bayg1239.
